title: The Room Map
subtitle: Each home now speaks, but the whole arrangement still lives in scattered pieces and in your head. The room map gathers the homes into a handful of zones, grouped by what you do, and makes the picture shared, so the entire room can be read at once. This completes Straighten.
part_position: Fourth and final chapter of Part Four (Straighten), chapters 12 to 15; it completes the second of the six S's and takes the last Straighten step
hands_off_note: Chapter 15 gathers the already-made, well-placed, self-explaining homes into a handful of zones by activity and turns the whole arrangement into one shared map, which reaches the Straighten-complete milestone. Sort cleared the room and Straighten arranged it; Chapter 16 opens Part Five (Shine), the third S, which cleans and cares for what remains and turns the simple act of cleaning into a way of noticing what needs attention before it becomes a problem.
audience: Readers who have finished Chapters 12 to 14, given every keeper a home, placed each home by how often they reach for it, and made each home explain itself, and are standing at the entryway where every home is now well chosen, well placed, and self-explaining, yet the whole arrangement still reads as separate clever spots and the picture that ties them together exists only in the head of the person who built it. Busy home keepers and parents. Applying the method, not new to it. They do not need to re-choose, re-place, or re-mark homes; they need to gather the homes into a few zones by activity and turn the whole arrangement into one shared map the household holds together.
core_promise: Complete Straighten by gathering the already-made, well-placed, self-explaining homes into a handful of zones grouped by activity, and turning the whole arrangement into one shared picture (the room map) that the household holds together. Learn what a room map is (a single shared picture of a space, organized into zones by the activities that happen there), group by what you do and not by what things are, recognize the entryway you have been building as one zone (the launch pad), and draw a simple map of your home's zones and walk the household through it, so the arrangement stops living in one person's head and starts living in the whole household, all without moving a single thing.
emotional_purpose: Carry the quiet pride of closing the second S, without hype. A private, in-your-head map is a natural stage, not a failing; it is where every well-run home sits right before this step. The reframe, the arrangement was yours and drawing the map together hands the design to the whole household, is meant to relieve and to share, not to scold: for as long as the arrangement lived only in your head you were on call to run it, and everyone else was a guest following rules they could feel but not see, and a shared map ends that. Deliver the honest STRAIGHTEN COMPLETE milestone: two of the six S's are done and the room is cleared and fully arranged, yet the goal is still ahead because four S's remain.
practical_purpose: Show why good, self-explaining homes can still add up to a scatter rather than a single view (each home was built one at a time and arranged around itself, not around the errands you actually run); define a room map and the garden or museum you-are-here diagram that names it; teach zones as the hero move (group by the verb, not the noun, so a coffee zone at the machine beats a kitchen things cupboard); reveal the running entryway example as one zone, the launch pad, then zoom out to the home as a handful of zones (coffee, homework corner, charging station, mail-and-admin); teach the two small acts that make the map shared (sketch it as a napkin diagram, then walk the household through it, from your room to their room); and read the friction meter as the STRAIGHTEN COMPLETE milestone, honest, with the goal still ahead.
primary_cta: Pick one busy corner and name, in a single word, the activity that happens there. Gather everything that activity needs into that spot, and move out anything that belongs to a different activity. You just drew your first zone. Read the chapter free in the online book.
secondary_cta: Read the chapter free online, then continue to Chapter 16, where Shine opens. Straighten has cleared and fully arranged the room; the third S now cleans and cares for what remains, and turns the simple act of cleaning into a way of noticing what needs attention before it becomes a problem.

worked_example.space: The finished entryway from Chapters 12 to 14, where every keeper has a good, well-placed, self-explaining home, yet the row still reads as separate clever spots with no single picture tying them together. In this pass the homes are gathered into named zones and the whole arrangement is drawn once and shared. Nothing moves house; the homes only gather into zones by activity and the map is made shareable.
worked_example.note: The entryway is one small hallway, but the same move scales to the whole home: five or six zones, each named for what happens there, describe almost any house. Nothing is added or removed; the homes just gather into a shared picture, so the room's logic stops being a private thing and becomes a public one.

zones.launch_pad: The entryway keepers (keys, leash, bag, umbrella, outgoing mail, shoes), revealed as one zone all along at the threshold between inside and out, everything the leaving-and-arriving activity needs clustered exactly where that activity happens.
zones.coffee: The mug, beans, grinder, and filters gathered at the machine, so making a cup collapses from a small circuit of the kitchen to a single reach, though nothing was bought and nothing thrown out.
zones.homework: Pens, paper, and a charger at the end of the dining table, the spot that becomes homework central at four o'clock.
zones.charging: The drawer and the power strip where every device charges overnight, wherever the household actually charges.
zones.mail_and_admin: The shelf near the front hall where the post lands and the bills get dealt with.

worked_example.drawing_and_sharing: Sketch the rough shape of a room, or the floor of the home, no straighter than a napkin diagram, and block in the zones. Then walk the household through it: stand in each zone in turn, say its name out loud, and let people put their hands on it. A child who has walked the map once can return the leash to the launch pad without being told.
worked_example.tally: Same keepers, same room, nothing added or removed, but the homes now gather into a handful of named zones and the picture is drawn where everyone can see it, so the whole room reads at a glance and the arrangement belongs to the household instead of living in one person's head.

definition: A room map is a single shared picture of a space, organized into zones by the activities that happen there, so anyone in the household can see where everything lives, and why, all at once.
zone_definition: A zone gathers everything one activity needs into the place that activity happens, so a task is served by one spot instead of scattered across the room.
one_idea_to_keep: Group the homes into a few zones by what you do, and draw the map once with everyone, so the arrangement stops living in your head and starts living in the whole household. A room whose logic is shared is a room that runs itself, which is exactly where Straighten set out to go.
